reader.title: Wild Horse pay-car incident
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Railroad section hands and laborers angry at a wage cut detained a company pay car and threatened its occupants; no report names a Black target or gives any racial framing (A1, A9, A19).

No one was killed: the wire version has a crowd threatening to lynch the railroad's manager, who was not present, and releasing the paymaster after he talked them down (A1, A19); the Dallas local report describes only a pay dispute with threats to the car (A9).

The wire and Dallas-special versions (A1, A19, A21) all appear to come from one Dallas source, while the Dallas Daily Herald's local account (A9) differs on the motive (unpaid wages, not Hoxie), length of detention (four or five hours, not two days) and makes no mention of a lynch threat.

summary.text: The Wild Horse pay-car incident was a confrontation in early January 1882 at Wild Horse station, Texas, in which section hands and laborers on the Texas & Pacific Railway stopped and held the company's pay car.

According to a widely reprinted telegraph story, the men took the car for that of General Manager Hoxie, whose order had cut their wages, and threatened to lynch him and burn the car before the paymaster talked them down.
No one was hurt, and a Dallas paper gave a different account in which the laborers were demanding unpaid wages and made no lynching threat.
Manager Hoxie had issued circulars reducing the pay of section hands and other laborers on the Texas & Pacific to $1.15 a day.
The pay car, carrying Paymaster Kretz and an assistant, made a monthly trip west along the line to settle with employes.

In the version carried by a Dallas special to the St. Louis Republican and by the St. Louis wire, a large body of laborers gathered at Wild Horse station, about 400 or 500 miles west of Dallas, mistook the pay car for Hoxie's private car and took Kretz for Hoxie.
They side-tracked the car and demanded that Hoxie be handed over "that they might lynch him," refusing to believe he was not aboard.
They then piled wood around the car to set it on fire and, in their reported words, "roast Hoxie out."
Kretz made a speech that calmed the crowd, but the men kept the car on the siding for forty-eight hours before letting it go east.
The St. Louis dispatch of January 13 placed the stoppage four days earlier, on the Monday before.
No arrests or official action appear in the coverage.

The wire added that discontent ran along the whole line, that a considerable number of mechanics had been discharged from the shops at Marshall, and that the men warned of "trouble" if a further general reduction went ahead.

The story spread by telegraph on January 14, 1882, under headlines such as "Desperate Railroaders" in the Memphis Daily Appeal, "Attempt to Burn a Paymaster" in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and "Got Hold of the Wrong Man" in the Portland Daily Press.
Papers from Salt Lake City to Wheeling and Savannah ran it within days, some garbling it so that Hoxie himself became the paymaster.
Reprints of the Dallas text were still appearing in early February, as in the Burrillville Gazette's "Burning a Paymaster."
Some papers used the episode for comment rather than news.

The Iron County Register in Missouri printed the Dallas special "as evidence of how the men feel toward Mr. Hoxie" inside an editorial calling him the most "universally" cursed railroad man in the country.
A St. Paul Pioneer-Press paragraph, reprinted in West Virginia, joked that the Southwest raised wages by holding the executive hostage and applying "hemp."
None of the coverage described the episode in racial terms.
The Dallas Daily Herald, citing the "colored porter" lately employed by Kretz, said the facts had been kept quiet for about ten days.

In its account an armed group of laborers at a station near El Paso halted the car because they were not on the pay list, threatened to destroy it, and let it go after four or five hours once Kretz convinced them of their error.
That local report mentions neither Hoxie nor any lynching threat, while the wire versions, which share wording and seem to come from a single Dallas source, rest on unnamed eyewitnesses.

accounts.label: Dallas special / St. Louis wire
accounts.gist: Laborers angry at Hoxie's wage cut mistook the pay car for his private car, demanded him for lynching, piled wood to burn the car, and held it 48 hours after Kretz pacified them; attributed to eyewitnesses after being 'kept from the reporters'.

accounts.label: Dallas Daily Herald local report (from Kretz's porter)
accounts.gist: Armed laborers near El Paso, left off the pay list, halted the car demanding pay, threatened to destroy it, and let it go after four or five hours when Kretz convinced them of their error.

framing.detail: Wire headlines such as 'Desperate Railroaders', 'Attempt to Burn a Paymaster' and 'Got Hold of the Wrong Man' presented the story as a sensational near-miss.
The Iron County Register cited the incident as 'evidence of how the men feel toward Mr. Hoxie' in an editorial condemning his treatment of employes.
A St. Paul Pioneer-Press paragraph mocked the mob's method of raising wages 'by an application of hemp'.
The Dallas Daily Herald's 'A Mob After a Pay-car' framed it as a pay dispute with no lynching threat.
